snippet.textDisplay: So the problem is if your parent doesn't have the financial ability to move into some kind of assisted living situation - then their only option is to stay in their home as long as possible. Many are right on the border line making maybe $100/month too much to qualify for Medicaid (about $2800/mo) and yet there's no way they can afford the $5000 to $8000/month or more required to live in various levels of assisted living. Selling a home can sometimes help, but often they still owe on it or they've borrowed against it to remain afloat. And often major investment needs to be made to update a house so it sells (lots of deferred maintenance) so you might have to try to come up with $50k or more just to get the house sellable. Meanwhile the elderly parent has to live somewhere while awaiting the money from the sale.

Despite setting boundaries - they never stick.
I wish I was the person who could walk away.
I finally retired and now I am living in this horrible situation.

We moved in with my parents believing it would be a supportive situation for everyone, especially as my mum has moderate dementia and my dad struggles with everyday tasks. I expected it to be challenging, but I didn’t anticipate how emotionally draining it would become.

Over time, boundaries and privacy have slowly eroded. Simple things like noise late at night, lack of respect for personal space, and dismissive reactions when concerns are raised have created constant tension. The hardest part has been seeing this spill over onto our 10-year old daughter, who is regularly made to feel guilty or shamed for not giving the level of attention they seem to expect from her.

She’s a child, yet there’s an unspoken pressure for her to perform emotionally to sit, engage, and meet adult needs even when she’s tired, unwell, or uncomfortable. Watching a child absorb that kind of expectation has been incredibly difficult, especially when attempts to gently set boundaries are met with tutting, resentment, or the reminder that “it’s our house.”

What this experience has taught me is that illness and struggle don’t automatically create empathy, and trying harder or being more accommodating doesn’t always improve things sometimes it makes the imbalance worse. This video really resonated because it put words to something I’ve been living with quietly: the slow exhaustion that comes from living in an environment where responsibility flows one way, but respect doesn’t.

snippet.textDisplay: my child was damaged with malpractice leaving her with a TBI and CP, non mobile, incontinent and essencially blind in a way. I get govnt steipend based on her medicare to care for her. I also have my aging parents living with me and they are both stroke survivors. One thing is the seclusion. Its hard to get out and socalize and damn near nobody ever shows up or reaches out to us. My mom had a TBI related type of dementia from child abuse she endured via her siblings growing up and thats really difficult to navigate for the household. I jokingly call myself "the snack bitch" bc i feel like im making all the choices for groceries. Im glad my parents still have control over their restroom needs, but the keeping track of finances, bills, the yardwork, the pets, etc. Its really a burnout marathon. I cry a lot. Im glad im there for my parents but i do think a lot about how nobody will be there for me when i need it and i feel MORE dread about my own future as an elderly person than i do about my caregiving. Im afraid of any of them (my kid or parents) outliving me bc they are not going to make it. Facilities are disgusting and short staffed and usually full of neglect (willful or not) and abuses (historically its always been that way) I always come back to the thought of hoping we all go at the same time somehow. Then im not leaving anyone who needs my care behind. This world is full of cruelty for elderly and disabled peoples and i fear a future for them without me to protect them all. I am glad that my parents are willing to go to facility under certian conditions we have talked about, at least they gave me that permission and strength.

snippet.textDisplay: Every situation is different. My dad retired from work at the age of 62 (young).  Just months after retiring, my dad got hit by a drunk driver and was in the CCU then ICU for a total of 2 months with a traumatic brain injury, which later turned into induced dementia.  My parents never got to enjoy their retirement together. He came home from the hospital with memory loss.  He did not even remember the accident, which was a good thing I guess.  He right away started showing signs of dementia.  His induced-dementia lasted for 21 years.  In the earlier stages of his dementia, some of the siblings started out trying to help my mom but our dad ran them off because he thought my brothers were strange men in his house while others just could not stand seeing their dad be mean like that.  He was very ugly and mean but it was all from the dementia.  He was a great father before the accident.  The latter stages of his dementia were the worst.  He was shitting constantly, accidentally smearing shit all over the place, spilling things, dropping things, falling down, crawling on the ground, repeating the same words all day, closing windows and locking doors during the daytime, and then opening windows and doors at night while my mom was sleeping.  By this time only a couple siblings were willing to help my mom with his care because of how ugly my dad was in the earlier stages of his dementia.  The last 3 years of his life was so bad that my mom and the 2 siblings just could not do it anymore.  We even had home care aides come in to try to help but eventually my mom ran them off because she did not like seeing different strangers in her house every day.  She insisted that she could do it without their help but she was in denial.  These home care aides did not look very professional and even looked shady at times.  In the very last stage of his dementia, my sister (POA) finally put him in a nursing home after discussing it with all the siblings. The pandemic hit about 9 months after he went into the nursing home.  He did not even last a year in the nursing home.  He was going to die anyway, but he just died quicker from the pandemic.  It was a long 20 or so years!!!!  My mom had a massive stroke on the day my dad died and then she passed away just 31 days after my dad from all the stress she endured while taking care of my dad.  We should have put him in a nursing home a lot sooner than later.  My mom had medical issues that we did not realize she had because we were all focused on dad for so long and NOT her.  She never told us she was having any significant health issues.  She kept her problems to herself.  So sad that we did not look out for our mom better than what we did!!!

snippet.textDisplay:
I absolutely agree. This hits very close to home.

My mother did finally agree to go into a care home, and lived there 7.5 years, gradually declining into dementia, and for the last 3 years needing nursing care, in bed. I felt so guilty I couldn’t do it, but I have chronic illness, so I’m glad I didn’t try, knowing I couldn’t but still feeling guilty. Then the chief nurse said not to be, that no one could do it alone. She reminded me they need a whole team, even though they do 12 hr shifts. No way. That helped me to be realistic.
Also that the toileting and bathing is better done by a carer (but preferably not a young man for an elderly woman! - that generation cares and so will I!). because that’s going to destroy the mother /daughter relationship and even more the mother/son.
You’re so right about fecal impaction - constipation is an absolute nightmare to manage.
I went to help Mum most days, and latterly every day and that exhausted me, 3-4 hr shifts. I managed the gaps that seemed to get forgotten, made sure things got done, fed her, cut and styled her hair, nails, shaved her, bathed her, kept her interested and clothed, supplied and amused, and endless conversation. When I was there the staff left me to it. I hope I did a good job, but I’m still exhausted, just from that. After she died I am executor and have her affairs to deal with, but at least they’re familiar because I managed them for her for over 15yrs! I’m in my 70s and she was 92.
Now I have nightmares about how my own end will be the same, fearing that my memory is going, and what it will be like to be left alone for hrs on end lying on a bunched up wet nighty with a tv channel I don’t want to watch. Or there’s no signal. But never mind because I can’t change the batteries in my hearing aids by myself and where are my glasses? I could really murd3r a cuppa and the food is so boring. I hope that bullying nurse isn’t on this afternoon. She got my meds wrong yesterday. When’s the doctor coming? Where is my daughter? She hasn’t been all week (oh yes she has). Who are you, dear? And worst of all, if your spouse is still alive, and also in care, why aren’t we together anymore?
Mum used to ask why she couldn’t come home with me, hating her fate. She imagined a rocking chair by the fire, helping with the veggies and talking my hind leg off. Such images would have her still my own age or younger, and me half her age, without grandchildren to fetch from school. In the end my sons moved away so the other grandmas could do the childminding, which is so sad.
The world has gone mad. We live too long, often dissociated from one another, and start our families too late. And perhaps needing two wages to pay our way doesn’t help us cope either.
A place in a care home costs an absolute fortune, yet the carers are on a basic wage.
Perhaps I won’t get the pneumonia protection when it’s offered. They used to call that the old dear’s friend - it takes you quietly Home.

snippet.textDisplay: Thanks for this video ! Lately I have seen a number of videos of people taking care of elderly, usually demented, parents at home. The vibe is how interesting and almost "fun" it is. It is not ! It is backbreaking, depressing and exhausting. My fear is with the current focus on cutting Medicaid ( over 60% of nursing home patients are paid for under the Medicaid program) families will have no option but to attempt home care. For those who are unaware, Medicare does NOT pay for routine assistance with daily living tasks ( toileting, bathing, dressing, feeding). Medicare only pays for "skilled care" which is specific types of care and then only for about 90 days. Many families are shocked to discover this and even more shocked when they discover the costs of nursing home care or even assisted living care.

snippet.textDisplay: I am a healthy 72 yo, cognitively fine, living alone for years, retired from corporate employment in a city that has had great value shifts.  Retired only because C19 shut down.  On the few occasions I allow myself to call for a sense of connection with people who know me, such as my brother and sister, I have experienced mostly conversations where I realize they are embarrassed and even hostile to me. For me, the sad time is when my sister and brother want to put me away, deny that I can garden, or do much of anything of interest, ignoring I supplied all cousins a year ago with heirloom seeds from my garden, recipes I had made, etc..  They, being 3 and 7 years younger, have me pegged for the last room at the end of the corridor, and be quiet.  While I am healthy, this is the staggering blow.  .When you have spent a lifetime devoted to satisfying corporate goals while subordinating your own , only to find that what you thought would be your blooming years, well, nobody cares whether you do or not.
